name: The Werther Effect
statement: Widely publicized suicides, especially of celebrities, are followed by a measurable spike in copycat suicides using similar methods.
statementAccent: a measurable spike in copycat suicides
meaning: The Werther effect describes documented increases in suicide rates following heavy media coverage of a suicide, particularly among people demographically similar to the deceased. It suggests media portrayal can act as a form of social suggestion or modelling that raises suicide risk in vulnerable individuals.
mechanism: Sociologist David Phillips proposed that publicised suicide stories provide a suggestive "script" that at-risk individuals imitate, with the size of the increase tied to the amount and prominence of coverage and concentrated near where the story ran. Effects are strongest among people similar in age or gender to the original case and typically occur within days to weeks.

examples.text: David P. Phillips’s 1974 paper in the American Sociological Review found US and British suicide rates rose immediately after front-page suicide stories between 1947 and 1968, with more coverage producing larger increases.
Following Marilyn Monroe’s publicised suicide, researchers documented an estimated 200 additional suicides above the seasonal average in the following month.
After South Korean actress Choi Jin-sil’s widely covered suicide, suicide rates in South Korea were reported to rise sharply in the ensuing period.

whyItMatters: The effect underlies media guidelines, such as WHO recommendations, urging responsible, non-sensationalised reporting of suicide — avoiding method details and prominent placement — to reduce contagion risk.
limits: Some high-profile deaths, such as Kurt Cobain’s in 1994, did not produce the expected spike, attributed partly to coverage that emphasised mental-health resources rather than romanticising the death (the protective "Papageno effect"). Effect sizes vary across studies, and isolating media causation from other social factors remains difficult.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as meaning any suicide reporting causes copycat deaths, when the research points specifically to sensationalised, front-page, or method-detailed coverage as the driver, with responsible reporting shown to blunt or reverse the effect.
origin: Coined by sociologist David P. Phillips in his 1974 American Sociological Review paper "The Influence of Suggestion on Suicide," named for the wave of copycat deaths reportedly following Goethe’s 1774 novel "The Sorrows of Young Werther."

sources.text: Copycat suicide, Wikipedia. — Phillips’s coinage, the Goethe-novel origin, and the Monroe and Choi Jin-sil cases.
Phillips, "The Influence of Suggestion on Suicide," American Sociological Review 39(3) (1974), JSTOR. — the original study naming the Werther effect.
